podcast.body: Released as The Clash's first single on March 18, 1977, this song was inspired by a real-life riot that occurred in the Notting Hill area of London the previous September. It addresses the institutional racism prevalent in Britain at the time and a controversial police action at the annual carnival held by West London's Caribbean community.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was directly inspired by the Notting Hill riot on August 30, 1976, where local black West Indian immigrants clashed with police. Joe Strummer was fascinated by the event, wondering why white people didn't show the same fortitude in fighting for their rights against the police. The song was misinterpreted by some as racist or an invitation to cause trouble, leading The Clash to stop playing it by the end of 1979, despite it becoming a classic. "Joe Strummer was fascinated by all this. He wondered why white people didn't have the same fortitude when standing up to police."

podcast.body: This song was inspired by the Notting Hill riot on August 30, 1976, where 1,600 police officers clashed with residents, resulting in 300 injured officers, 35 overturned police vehicles, property damage, and 66 arrests. Joe Strummer was fascinated by the fortitude of the Black West Indian community who fought back against police harassment and questioned why white people didn't show the same resolve. The band stopped playing the song by the end of 1979 due to misinterpretation, with some calling it racist or taking it as an invitation to cause trouble, but it remained a Clash classic. "But that didn't stop it from becoming a clash classic."
